newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Money launderers are getting smarter-anaylsts.
newsitem.headline: Money launderers are getting smarter-anaylsts.

text.p: Criminals are constantly finding new ways to siphon proceeds from their activities into legitimate businesses, delegates at a money laundering conference said on Monday.

"Ironically, the more countries enact laws that allow the profit of crime to be taken away, the greater the incentive there is for criminals to embark on even more sophisticated money laundering operations," said Graham Saltmarsh, from the Directorate of Intelligence at London's New Scotland Yard.
The two-day international conference in Cyprus's capital Nicosia is organised by International Business Communications' (IBC) Gulf Conferences group.

According to most estimates, the amount of money laundered each year exceeds $500 billion, while some argue that it probably reaches $1 trillion, Cyprus Central Bank Governor Afxentis Afxentiou said in a keynote address.
"At such levels the amount of money laundered is almost equivalent to the annual GDP of some of the largest western European states," he said.
Almost 70 percent of illicit funds are believed to be drug-related.
Jonathan Polk, Counsel at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, said banking institutions were the first, and the last, line of defence against money laundering.
But he said non-banking institutions like money remitting services and insurance companies in the U.S. were also being used to legalise illicit gains.

"A money launderer can go to an (insurance) agent and take a premium bond which is then posted as collateral for a loan, or sells it at a discount. It is an efficient way of turning dirty money into clean money," he said.
Saltmarsh named the Japanese Yakuza, the Chinese Triads, the Columbian cartels and the Sicilian Mafia as the four main crime gangs.
Russia, he said, now has an established organised crime problem which is worrying.
While not all of it is connected to crime proceeds, there are "a lot of Russians with a lot of ready cash for investments", he said.
Counting some 2,600 gangs now operational in the Russian Federation, Saltmarsh said the largest and most feared was the "Chechenskaya Mafia".
"It is this group that worries us. It is this group that has branched into upper world businesses which includes casinos, restaurants, nightclubs, and even food and consumer groups.
They have moved on into international extortion, loan sharking and money laundering and they are unafraid to reach out internationally," said Saltmarsh.

Delegates at the conference, who were mainly regional bankers, were urged to keep their staff trained to spot any discrepancies in transactions and to adopt rigid "know your customer" rules, even if thorough background checks discouraged potential legitimate clients.
"The alternative to that is having them possibly selling drugs to your children," said Polk.
